The life cycle of Dolioletta gegenbauri begins with the release of a fertilized egg that rapidly develops into a free-swimming larva. At a stable temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], these larvae appear less than 24 hours after egg release, giving an age at birth of approximately 1 day [ab = approximately 1 day]. This larva then metamorphoses into the oozooid stage, the initial asexual generation. Upon its emergence, the early oozooid measures just 0.1 cm [Lb = 0.1 cm] in length, marking the length at birth for the asexual cycle. Within about five days, this founder individual develops a distinctive cadophore, a thread-like posterior extension that will carry the next generation. Along this cadophore, tiny feeding units called trophozooids begin to bud, typically starting with just two such individuals. These trophozooids are critical for sustaining the colony, capturing food particles that nourish the entire integrated structure. The initial size of the oozooid is remarkably small, reflecting the rapid pace of early development that characterizes the fast life history of these pelagic tunicates.

The asexual generation of D. gegenbauri progresses through a complex colonial organization. The trophozooids that bud from the oozooid's cadophore continue to develop, and the colony eventually produces phorozooids, which serve as protective transporters for the sexual stage. Under laboratory conditions maintained at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the average lifespan of a nurse oozooid is 20.2 days [am = 20.2 days], after which it senesces and dies. During its relatively brief existence, a single phorozooid achieves an ultimate length of 1.0 cm [Li = 1.0 cm] at full maturity. The phorozooid does not reproduce itself, but rather acts as a host. It was observed that the first gonozooids, which are the sexual generation, are released when the phorozooid reaches a length of 5 mm, which corresponds to a length at puberty for the asexual generation of 0.5 cm [Lp = 0.5 cm]. This release marks the transition from the purely somatic functions of the colony to the initiation of sexual reproduction.

The released gonozooids represent the sexual generation of the doliolid, and they are miniature at the time of their liberation. These newly freed individuals have a length at birth of approximately 0.15 cm [Lb = approximately 0.15 cm], falling within the reported range of 1 to 2 mm. At this small size, they must quickly mature to begin their reproductive role. The reproductive output of the gonozooid is prodigious at the standard temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. Each mature gonozooid can release eggs at a rate that equates to a maximum reproductive rate of approximately 28 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 28 eggs per day] for the sexual generation. The initiation of this egg shedding event is tied to body size; the start of egg release by the gonozooids occurs once they attain a length at puberty for the sexual generation of 0.6 cm [Lp = 0.6 cm]. This size milestone ensures that the individual has the somatic resources necessary to support the energetically demanding process of repeated spawning.

In addition to the high egg output of the gonozooids, the phorozooids also exhibit a significant asexual reproductive capacity. The number of gonozooids produced by a single phorozooid during its life span varies, with reported totals ranging from 83 to 163 individuals. This translates to a maximum reproductive rate for the asexual generation of 11 gonozooids per day [Ri = 11 gonozooids per day] when measured at the same thermal regime of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. The timing of this asexual production is tightly regulated. Approximately 4 days after the phorozooid itself is released from the nurse colony, it becomes capable of releasing its first gonozooids. This interval defines the time since birth at puberty for the phorozooid, which is exactly 4 days [tp = 4 days] at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This rapid transition from release to reproductive activity underscores the species' strategy of high turnover, maximizing the number of offspring produced within its brief lifespan.

The coordinated life cycle of D. gegenbauri is an impressive example of polymorphism and ecological optimization. The sequential development from oozooid to phorozooid to gonozooid allows for a division of labor within the colony. The first gonozooids are released by the phorozooids very quickly, emphasizing that the phorozooid life stage acts primarily as a vehicle for disseminating the sexual generation. The 20.2-day maximum lifespan (20.2 days) [am = 20.2 days] recorded at 20 °C [T = 20 °C] places Dolioletta gegenbauri among the shorter-lived gelatinous zooplankton, a trait consistent with its rapid colonial turnover and high fecundity. This short generation time is typical of gelatinous zooplankton, allowing populations to respond rapidly to favorable environmental conditions. The small size of the early oozooid and the rapid onset of reproduction in both the asexual and sexual phases are key adaptations for a planktonic existence where mortality is high and resource patches are ephemeral. The entire cycle is energetically driven by the feeding activity of the trophozooids, making the colony a highly integrated superorganism.
